transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what's been bothering you and what brought you in today?

Hi. Thank you for seeing me. I... well, I guess I'm here because I just don't know what else to do at this point. I came in because I can’t shake this heavy, just completely hopeless feeling. It’s... it's hard to explain, but it’s like, you know, after my divorce, I worked so incredibly hard to put my life back together. I’m a civil engineer, so I guess I naturally look at things like a project. I laid a new foundation, I got my routines in place, I really thought I had constructed this stable, solid life for myself. 

But lately... I don't know, it feels like everything I built after the divorce has just completely collapsed. All of it. And I’m just sitting under it. Like I'm trapped under all this rubble and concrete, and the weight of it is just so heavy. I can't even breathe, let alone try to figure out how to rebuild again. I just sit there under the weight of it all. I try to tell myself to just get up and push through, to be logical about it, but the hopelessness is just so overwhelming that I end up just... stuck. I just can't shake it, no matter what I do, and I don't know how to get out from under it anymore.
How long have you been feeling this way—this heavy, hopeless feeling you're describing?

Well, it’s been... I’d say it’s been hanging over me for about a month now. Maybe a little over four weeks. It really all started right around the time the financial mess from the divorce finally hit me. 

You see, when you go through something like that, everyone warns you about the emotional toll, but no one really prepares you for the absolute logistical nightmare of untangling a life. We had lawyers going back and forth, and suddenly I was looking at all these hidden debts and legal fees that somehow fell squarely on my shoulders. I remember the exact day it happened, about a month ago. I was sitting at my kitchen island with all my spreadsheets open—because, like I said, I try to map everything out, I try to calculate the load and budget for the stress—and I just realized the math wasn't going to work. The financial hole was just too deep. 

And that’s when this... this massive cloud just descended on me. Ever since that specific afternoon, every single day for the last month, I wake up and that concrete rubble feeling is already there, pressing down on my chest before I even open my eyes. I just keep replaying the numbers and the meetings with the lawyers, and it’s just this constant, unrelenting weight. I thought I had accounted for everything, but that financial fallout just broke the supports I had built, and... yeah. It’s been a solid month of just being completely crushed under it. I just can't seem to find a way to engineer a way out of a deficit like this, emotionally or financially.
Aside from the divorce and financial situation, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in other things you used to enjoy—like hobbies, work projects, or time with friends?

No, I mean... I haven't really noticed anything like that. It's just... I guess I don't really know what you mean. I mean, work is still work, you know? I still go in, I still look at the blueprints, I still run the structural analysis software. It's not like I suddenly hate engineering. I've always loved the precision of it, the way you can calculate exact load-bearing capacities and know for a fact whether a bridge will stand or fall. That certainty has always been really comforting to me, especially when everything else in my life feels so unpredictable. So, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest in my work projects. 

And as for hobbies... well, I used to do a lot of drafting for fun, just sketching out theoretical structures, like these really intricate, sustainable urban housing models. I haven't really done much of that lately, but I think that's just because I'm so exhausted from the financial stress, not because I don't enjoy it anymore. It's just hard to find the energy to pick up a drafting pencil when you're spending all your free time looking at bank statements and lawyer bills, trying to figure out how you're going to pay for groceries next week. 

And friends... I mean, I still have friends. I still text them. Sarah, my best friend from college, she's been checking in on me a lot since the divorce. She actually works in finance, so she's been trying to help me make sense of some of the debt restructuring options, which is incredibly kind of her. We used to get coffee every Sunday morning at this little place downtown, the one with the really good almond croissants, but we haven't done that in a few weeks. But again, that's mostly just because I've been so bogged down with the paperwork and the sheer exhaustion of it all. It's not that I don't want to see her or that I don't enjoy her company. I do. It's just... the logistics of leaving the house and pretending everything is fine when I'm carrying this massive, concrete weight on my chest... it just feels like too much effort right now. So, no, I wouldn't say I've lost pleasure in those things. It's just the circumstances, you know? The circumstances are just taking up all my bandwidth.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep over the past month—trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or sleeping much more than usual?

Well, sleep... sleep has become its own kind of project, honestly, and one that I am completely failing at. It’s like my brain refuses to power down. I’d say for the last month, it’s been this agonizing cycle. I get into bed, I turn off the lamp, I try to do that deep breathing thing my sister told me about, but the second the room is dark, it’s like someone flips a switch in my head and the projector turns on. 

I just lie there, wide awake, staring up at the ceiling, and my mind just starts running through every single bill, every line item on the lawyer's invoice, trying to recalculate the deficit. And then, if I manage to push the financial stuff away, my brain decides it's time to review every structural analysis I did that day at work, obsessing over whether I missed a stress fracture in the steel beams for that new overpass project, or if my load calculations were off by a fraction of a percent. It’s just this endless loop of worry. 

And then, if I finally do manage to drift off—usually from sheer exhaustion around 2 or 3 in the morning—I don’t stay asleep. I’ll jolt awake before dawn, like 4:30 or 5:00 AM, and my heart is just pounding. I wake up feeling completely drained, like I never actually slept at all, like my brain was still running calculations all night while my eyes were closed. I just lie there in the dark, watching the clock change, knowing I have to get up and face another day feeling like I'm carrying a ton of concrete, but I just don't have the energy to even pull the covers off. So, yeah, I guess you could say I’m having a lot of trouble falling asleep, and staying asleep... it’s just completely broken right now.
Have you been experiencing feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt—like feeling like you're a failure or that this is somehow your fault beyond just the financial situation—over the past month?

Yeah... yeah, it’s... it’s constant. It goes so far beyond just the money. The money is just the math, but the feeling behind it, it’s like this core belief now that I am just fundamentally broken. I keep telling myself that I’m a failed wife, for one. You know, you build a life with someone, you lay a foundation, and when the whole thing collapses into rubble, you have to look at who designed it, right? And I just feel like it’s all my fault. I couldn't hold it together. 

And it bleeds into everything else. I sit at my desk at work and I just stare at the screen, thinking about how I’m a terrible engineer. I mean, if I can’t even engineer my own personal life to withstand basic stress tests, how can anyone trust me to calculate the shear strength of a retaining wall? It’s pathetic. I just feel like this massive burden to everyone around me. Like Sarah, my friend I mentioned earlier, she’s so nice to me, she tries so hard to help, but I know I’m just dragging her down. I’m a burden to her, I’m a burden to my firm, to my ex... to everyone. 

And my brain, it won't let it go. It just constantly collects evidence to support how awful I am. I will literally sit there and replay every single tiny mistake I've ever made. A missed calculation on a preliminary draft from months ago, or... or a tense email I sent to a project manager where I was maybe a little too abrupt. I’ll just loop that one email in my head for hours, analyzing every single word, using it as absolute, undeniable proof that I just ruin things. I ruin everything I touch. It’s like I have this inherent structural flaw in my character, and no matter how much I try to patch it or reinforce it, I’m just destined to fail and make a mess of everything. It’s just this overwhelming guilt that I can't logic my way out of, because my brain keeps serving up the evidence, you know? The tense emails, the math errors, the divorce papers... it’s all just proof that I'm a failure.
Over this past month, have you had any thoughts of wanting to hurt yourself, that you'd be better off dead, or of not wanting to go on living?

I... honestly... yeah. I have. It’s hard to even say out loud because, you know, as an engineer, you’re supposed to fix problems, you're supposed to reinforce the weak points, not... not just want to abandon the project entirely. But lately, especially when I’m lying awake at 4 or 5 in the morning like I was telling you about, just staring at the dark and feeling that massive concrete weight on my chest... I just... I’ve been having these thoughts that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. 

Like, if I could just go to sleep and the whole system would just power down permanently. No more recalculating the debt, no more feeling like a complete failure, no more dragging Sarah down with my mess. Just... quiet. Zero load. And for a while, it was just sort of this passive wish, you know? Just this exhausting sigh in the dark where I'd think about how nice it would be to just not have to do any of this anymore.

But then... I guess it was last Tuesday? Or Wednesday, the days are kind of blurring together with the lack of sleep. But the thoughts, they got really, really intense. It wasn't just a passive wish anymore; my brain started presenting it as a logical solution, which is what really terrified me. I was sitting at my desk, looking at the specs for this overpass, and my brain was just telling me over and over that everyone would be better off, that the math actually made sense if I just wasn't here to ruin things anymore. 

It got so loud and so heavy that I actually really scared myself. I realized I was standing on the edge of a total structural collapse and I didn't even want to stop it. I couldn't put that on Sarah—she's already dealing with enough of my baggage—so I actually ended up digging through the HR portal on my work computer. I found the number for our Employee Assistance Program, and I called them right there from my office with the door closed. I just... I had to do something, I had to talk to someone right that second because being alone with those thoughts when they get that intense and start making sense to you... it’s just terrifying. So, yes. I have been thinking about it.
Right now, do you have any specific plan for how you might end your life, or access to something you could use to do it?

Well, like I was just saying, it... it really has always been more about just wishing I wouldn't wake up. As far as a specific, actionable plan, you know, like a blueprint or a step-by-step schematic of how to actually execute it... no, I don't have that. I mean, I'm an engineer, right? If I were going to actually do something, my brain would probably obsess over the logistics and the variables of it, but it hasn't been like that. It’s just been this crushing, suffocating weight where my brain screams that it would just be so much easier to not be here. 

And... and that's exactly why I ended up calling that Employee Assistance Program line last week. Because even without a... a fully drafted plan or, you know, access to something specific sitting right there on my desk, the thoughts themselves just got so incredibly intense. They got so loud and started making so much sense to me that I genuinely scared myself. I didn't have a weapon or anything, it was just the sheer force of the logic my brain was throwing at me, telling me the math works out better for everyone if I'm just gone. 

So instead of figuring out the "how," I just panicked and dialed that number. Because I knew if I sat there in my office any longer, just letting that twisted logic build and build, I might actually cross that line and start figuring out a method. I just... I had to interrupt the circuit before I started planning the structural failure, if that makes sense. So, no, I don't have a specific plan right now, or access to anything, just... just that really terrifying intensity that I'm still trying to outrun.

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been thinking that it would be easier if I didn’t wake up, and the thoughts got intense enough that I scared myself and called the employee assistance program.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of wanting to hurt myself, being better off dead, or not wanting to go on living, which directly corresponds to the Death/Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
I... honestly... yeah. I have. It’s hard to even say out loud because, you know, as an engineer, you’re supposed to fix problems, you're supposed to reinforce the weak points, not... not just want to abandon the project entirely. But lately, especially when I’m lying awake at 4 or 5 in the morning like I was telling you about, just staring at the dark and feeling that massive concrete weight on my chest... I just... I’ve been having these thoughts that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. 

Like, if I could just go to sleep and the whole system would just power down permanently. No more recalculating the debt, no more feeling like a complete failure, no more dragging Sarah down with my mess. Just... quiet. Zero load. And for a while, it was just sort of this passive wish, you know? Just this exhausting sigh in the dark where I'd think about how nice it would be to just not have to do any of this anymore.

But then... I guess it was last Tuesday? Or Wednesday, the days are kind of blurring together with the lack of sleep. But the thoughts, they got really, really intense. It wasn't just a passive wish anymore; my brain started presenting it as a logical solution, which is what really terrified me. I was sitting at my desk, looking at the specs for this overpass, and my brain was just telling me over and over that everyone would be better off, that the math actually made sense if I just wasn't here to ruin things anymore. 

It got so loud and so heavy that I actually really scared myself. I realized I was standing on the edge of a total structural collapse and I didn't even want to stop it. I couldn't put that on Sarah—she's already dealing with enough of my baggage—so I actually ended up digging through the HR portal on my work computer. I found the number for our Employee Assistance Program, and I called them right there from my office with the door closed. I just... I had to do something, I had to talk to someone right that second because being alone with those thoughts when they get that intense and start making sense to you... it’s just terrifying. So, yes. I have been thinking about it.

inference.note: The patient now endorses pervasive depressed mood, insomnia, guilt/worthlessness, and active suicidal ideation with a recent intense episode requiring crisis intervention, fulfilling full criteria for a major depressive episode of at least moderate-severe intensity. This depth and duration of symptoms (mood, cognition, sleep, guilt, SI) exceed what's expected for adjustment disorder, so F43.21 is ruled out. Severity now suggests F32.2 rather than unspecified F32.9.

doctor.intent: Assess current suicide risk severity, including whether she has a specific plan, means, or intent to act on these thoughts now
doctor.question: Right now, do you have any specific plan for how you might end your life, or access to something you could use to do it?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been thinking that it would be easier if I didn’t wake up, and the thoughts got intense enough that I scared myself and called the employee assistance program.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a follow-up question about suicidal plans and access to means, which falls under the assessment of suicidal ideation and intent.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying, it... it really has always been more about just wishing I wouldn't wake up. As far as a specific, actionable plan, you know, like a blueprint or a step-by-step schematic of how to actually execute it... no, I don't have that. I mean, I'm an engineer, right? If I were going to actually do something, my brain would probably obsess over the logistics and the variables of it, but it hasn't been like that. It’s just been this crushing, suffocating weight where my brain screams that it would just be so much easier to not be here. 

And... and that's exactly why I ended up calling that Employee Assistance Program line last week. Because even without a... a fully drafted plan or, you know, access to something specific sitting right there on my desk, the thoughts themselves just got so incredibly intense. They got so loud and started making so much sense to me that I genuinely scared myself. I didn't have a weapon or anything, it was just the sheer force of the logic my brain was throwing at me, telling me the math works out better for everyone if I'm just gone. 

So instead of figuring out the "how," I just panicked and dialed that number. Because I knew if I sat there in my office any longer, just letting that twisted logic build and build, I might actually cross that line and start figuring out a method. I just... I had to interrupt the circuit before I started planning the structural failure, if that makes sense. So, no, I don't have a specific plan right now, or access to anything, just... just that really terrifying intensity that I'm still trying to outrun.

inference.note: Patient endorses persistent depressed mood, sleep disturbance (initial and early morning waking), pervasive worthlessness/guilt, and both passive and near-active suicidal ideation with recent crisis-level intensity, all lasting over a month following an identifiable stressor. Though anhedonia is denied, the number and severity of symptoms (including significant suicidality prompting a crisis call) meet criteria for a single major depressive episode, severe, without psychotic features. This exceeds the threshold for adjustment disorder given symptom severity and SI, and there is no evidence of manic/hypomanic history or psychotic features to broaden the differential.
